title: {{NAME}} and the Clockwork Fairy Garden
moral: True friendship means helping someone shine, even when it means stepping back yourself.

pages.content:
The Whirring Wood stretched out before {{NAME}} like a dream someone had forgotten to finish. Copper trees twisted upward, their leaves thin as foil and trembling in a warm electric breeze. Tiny lights blinked between the branches, and somewhere deep in the humming shadows, a bell chimed in a rhythm that sounded almost like a heartbeat.

It had started, as extraordinary things often do, with a hole in the garden wall. {{NAME}} had squeezed through expecting nettles. Instead, he found this, a forest that smelled of warm circuits and wild honeysuckle all at once.

Robots no bigger than squirrels scurried along the roots, carrying dewdrops in thimble-sized buckets. Mechanical butterflies with shimmering wing-panels drifted overhead, trailing threads of silver light. And hovering just above a mossy boulder, a tiny winged figure no larger than a teacup was bent over a broken clockwork flower, muttering furiously to herself.

pages.content:
The fairy looked up, and {{NAME}} saw that her wings were unlike anything he had imagined. They were not gauzy or delicate. They were made of interlocking cogs and micro-panels, spinning in two different directions at once, catching the light like a tiny stained-glass window in motion.

"You're not supposed to be here," she announced, though she didn't sound particularly alarmed. Her name, she explained with great dignity, was Copperwing, and she was the Royal Engineer of the Fairy Mechanism, the hidden heart of the entire wood that kept every robot, every blossom, and every beam of magical light running perfectly.

Except today it wasn't running perfectly at all.

"The main drive-spring has snapped," Copperwing said, holding up a coil of broken wire no thicker than a thread. Her amber eyes were bright but tired. "Without it, the whole garden will go dark before midnight." She looked at {{NAME}} with the frank assessment of someone who had very little time to waste. "Do you know anything about fixing things?"

pages.content:
They moved fast. Copperwing led {{NAME}} at a run, ducking under arches of woven wire and leaping over streams that ran with liquid that glowed faintly violet. The Fairy Mechanism turned out to be a magnificent tower of interlocking gears in the very centre of the wood, tall as a house and humming with a sound like a thousand music boxes playing at once.

With Copperwing directing from his shoulder, {{NAME}} climbed. Hand over hand, gear over gear. A small helper-robot named Pip, round as a football and painted cherry red, clanged along beside him, passing tools with its magnetic claw. Bolts flew. Springs uncoiled and were wound again. {{NAME}}'s hands worked while Copperwing sang a repair-spell in a voice like a plucked harp string, her wings spinning faster and faster as the magic built.

Then, with a creak and a tremendous CLANG that sent a flock of mechanical starlings bursting into the sky, the new spring locked into place. The tower shuddered, groaned, and began to spin.

pages.content:
But something was wrong. The tower was spinning too fast. A deep groan resonated through the copper trees, and one by one the lights around the wood began to flicker. Pip let out a whistle of alarm. Copperwing's wings locked rigid with shock.

"The calibration dial," she breathed. "It needs to be turned to precisely the seventh notch, or the whole mechanism will overwind and shatter."

The dial was at the very top of the tower. It was also glowing a dangerous, pulsing red.

{{NAME}} looked up. He looked at Copperwing. Without a word, he pulled his LED trainer from his foot, unthreaded the lace, and looped it around a high gear-spoke to create a handhold where none had existed. Then he climbed, hand over trembling hand, the tower vibrating around him like a giant struck bell.

With both hands he gripped the dial. One, two, three, four, five, six, SEVEN. A sound like a chorus of crystal glasses rang out across the wood. The glow shifted from red to a deep, pulsing, glorious gold.

pages.content:
The Whirring Wood came alive all at once, a cascade of light rolling through every copper tree like a sunrise made of clockwork. Flowers bloomed in sequences of pink and gold. Pip spun in dizzy circles of joy, his little red body clanging softly against the roots. The robot squirrels cheered in tiny electronic voices.

Copperwing landed on {{NAME}}'s knee as he sat against the warm base of the tower, breathing slowly. She pressed one small, gear-winged hand against his thumb. It was a very serious gesture for someone the size of a teacup, and {{NAME}} understood it completely.

The walk home felt shorter somehow, the ordinary garden glowing a little in the corners where the light slanted just right. {{NAME}} curled beneath his covers, warm and pleasantly tired, still feeling the faint vibration of a thousand gears in his fingertips.

He closed his eyes. And somewhere in the warm dark behind his eyelids, he was almost certain he could see a tiny amber light, blinking slowly. Waiting for morning.
